lignes.texte: Microsoft is actively sabotaging your computer. For 20 years, VLC media player opened instantly.
Then overnight, double clicking it suddenly triggered a brutal freeze. The internet
immediately turned on open source developers, claiming the software had become bloated garbage.
But the code hadn’t changed at all. It was something darker. Something more sinister.
Microsoft’s security teams were conducting systematic sweeps and suffocating the app from the
inside out. But VLC was just the first casualty. This software kill squad is only getting started.
And their next target… is already on your laptop. The crisis exploded in August 2026. Users noticed
that VLC was taking up to 33 seconds to begin playing a basic MP3 on some Windows 11 machines.
That delay would be annoying on a 10-year-old laptop.
But this wasn’t some older hardware. One affected user was running one of
the fastest gaming processors money can buy. And it was struggling with a format from the 1990s.
An MP3 is so fundamentally basic, every phone, car stereo, and smart speaker can
play it without breaking a sweat. Decoding it should take a fraction of a second.
Instead, it was bringing modern computers to their knees.
The issue might have stayed buried. A niche complaint on forums that people
discussed then forgot about. Instead, it found a megaphone.
Jonathan Blow, the programmer behind the acclaimed puzzle games Braid and The Witness, publicly
announced that he had dropped VLC. The delay had made him switch to Microsoft’s Media Player.
Then he went further. In his view, “a large sector of open-source
software is in a truly embarrassing place now.” It was a devastating verdict from an industry
heavyweight. And it landed on a project that didn’t deserve it.
Because when a state of the art PC takes half a minute to open an audio file,
there are really only two suspects. Either the program is broken,
or the system underneath it is. VLC’s developers didn’t take it
lying down. On August 12th, they fired back. According to them, the delay was caused by an
issue caused by Microsoft’s antivirus program Defender. The problem was introduced through a
Windows 11 update that had quarantined the critical start-up files VLC needed to run.
They intentionally put the word “bug” in quotation marks. A subtle way of
suggesting that this wasn’t an accident. It was how Windows wanted to do things.
To top it off, they took a shot at Jonathan Blow, calling it “quite disrespectful” to brand
open source software embarrassing, especially over an issue that a Windows update caused.
The code hadn’t gone bad. Something inside Windows had started treating
a normal part of VLC like a threat. Blow wasn’t convinced. He argued that fixing
the problem was the developer’s responsibility. He pointed out that he personally patched his game,
Braid, after AMD caused an issue. Maybe he had a point, but the 2 situations aren’t the same.
Braid is a commercial game. When it works, its creator gets paid.
VLC is a different animal. It’s overseen by VideoLAN, a nonprofit with no
permanent employees. It runs mostly on volunteers and donations. And it has stayed that way on
purpose. VLC’s longtime lead, Jean-Baptiste Kempf, has spent years turning down multi-million dollar
buyouts and venture capital. He refused to adopt a model that didn’t bring value for the users.
It’s that integrity that earned VLC its reputation. For a whole generation of users,
VLC is the first program they install on a new laptop because
it spent decades rejecting the ads, bundles and corporate tracking that no one asked for.
So on one side, you have a volunteer-driven project that walked away from a small fortune
to keep its software clean. On the other side, you have one of the largest companies on Earth,
shipping the operating system, the antivirus, and, conveniently,
the rival media player Blow switched to. Someone was lying. And it came down to
what was happening behind the scenes. VLC is able to run quickly because it uses
a master catalog. A single file that tells the app where its tools are so it can open them quickly.
It’s like a massive library. When you want a book, the librarian doesn’t search every aisle.
They check the database and go straight to the correct shelf.
That catalog is what allows it to skip rescanning its entire start up folder every time it opens.
But Windows turned Microsoft Defender into a paranoid guard. Instead of letting VLC
read its own catalog, Defender locked the files away. It forced your computer
to manually stop and inspect every piece of data before letting the app begin its tasks.
The media player was fine. The files were fine. But Microsoft’s digital bouncer was blocking the
door and id’ing everyone who tried to get in. Checking files is Defender’s job. Microsoft
updates its security fingerprints regularly to catch malware. But if a corporate giant
tells its bouncer to be overzealous, safe independent software starts to look like a virus.
That’s what seems to have happened here. When Defender quarantines or blocks VLC’s
start up files, it forces the player to grind through its system every time you click a file.
But Microsoft never acknowledged it. There was no official statement or fix. Tech reports traced it
back to a buggy security fingerprint update. But because no one actually commented on it,
users were left in the dark and blaming the app. If it was a one-time glitch,
you could shrug it off. Software breaks. Updates go wrong.
But the problem isn’t new. Complaints go back to 2025,
buried in a Reddit thread title “Start of VLC slowed by Windows Defender”.
One Windows 10 user described a 24-second delay that vanished once VLC had been opened,
only to return after the PC sat idle. Dozens of other users joined in, reporting the same freeze
across Windows 10 and Windows 11 editions. So this isn’t strictly a Windows 11 issue.
It spans 2 versions of Windows and multiple VLC releases. The problem
isn’t a broken piece of media software. It’s the aggressive security layer underneath it.
It’s also maddeningly inconsistent. When a tech-oriented news outlet tried to reproduce it,
VLC launched normally on their Windows 11 test machine. One user reported that the stall only
strikes the first file after a reboot, and never the one after it. And that inconsistency
is exactly why open source software takes the fall. When a program freezes in front of you,
you blame the program. Almost nobody thinks to blame the antivirus working in the background.
VLC isn’t the only independent Windows program living with this.
Paint.NET, a free image editor that started as a student project, has run into Defender more
than once. Users realized that adding the app’s folder to Defender’s exclusion list
instantly fixed their performance issues. Things got so bad, the developer had to
rewrite an message to give the real reason files weren’t saving: Windows Defender.
An independent developer had to signpost an error just so users wouldn’t blame his app.
Years earlier, right after a major Windows 10 update, one user on its forum reported
the editor taking several minutes to become responsive when opening or creating an image.
Think about that for a second. An independent developer spent time rewriting an error message
so users would stop blaming his app for something Windows was doing.
It’s a common pattern. Windows’ own security layer trips up the software, and the independent app
wears the blame. Breaking that pattern takes evidence that points in only one direction.
The smoking gun came from an X user who recorded themselves opening an MP3 with VLC,
but on a Linux system. It didn’t take 33 seconds. It took 1.
It’s the exact same program, playing the exact same file. You don’t need
a lab test to see what’s happening. The operating system is the problem.
When you tell Windows to ignore VLC, the player opens instantly. The only difference was whether
Window’s digital bouncer was standing in the way. The irony is that while people like Jonathan Blow
were criticizing VLC, Microsoft’s own Media Player was coming under scrutiny. Just months earlier,
Windows Latest had tested it and found it was the slower, heavier option. It took noticeably
longer than VLC to open a video, ate up massive amounts of memory and struggled with basic files.
So a developer frustrated by slowness abandoned a program that was being slowed down by Windows,
and replaced it with a Microsoft program that was fundamentally slower. Whatever the reason,
the immediate result was exactly what Microsoft wanted. Users moved from an
independent app to Window’s own player. So, is VLC a fluke, or a glimpse of how
Windows treats software that gets in its way. Microsoft Edge is less browser and more parasite
in your system. If you tell Windows you want to use Chrome or Firefox, updates will routinely
reset your default settings. If you try to delete Edge, parts of it keep running in the background.
Even when your choice of default browser sticks, Windows cheats.
Parts of Windows 10 and 11 completely ignore the default browser and force links open in Edge. For
new PCs, Edge might also be tied to other formats like PDFs over full-fledged readers like Adobe,
without asking your permission. Microsoft can fix this.
In fact, it already has… for some people. To comply with the European Union’s Digital
Markets Act, Windows suddenly learned to respect user choices. For European users,
Edge and Bing became easy to uninstall. The European rules went further still.
Clicking “Set default” for a rival browser now covers far more link and file types,
including PDFs. They even stripped out the “Featured app” box that
used to promote Edge whenever someone tried to change their browser defaults,
and that change reached users worldwide. Every one of these moves proves the same thing:
when Microsoft is legally required to give competitors a level playing field, it can.
Which means everything on your laptop is a deliberate choice.
The same two-tier treatment shows up in less obvious places. If you download an app from
the Window’s store, it automatically gets the VIP treatment to launch immediately. But do the same
thing with an app like VLC, and Windows hides it behind a wall of code. It forces users to manually
hack their own registry files to find it It gets worse.
Python is one of the world’s most popular programming languages. Windows includes shortcuts
that hijacks Python and Python3 commands and diverts them to the Microsoft Store. It forces you
to go into settings and clean up Microsoft’s mess. And while VLC was freezing,
Microsoft dropped another bombshell. In August 2026, Microsoft announced a
mandatory security update. Within days, video games were crashing and forcing PCs to reboot.
Developers like Embark had to put emergency warnings on Discord, stating that Windows
was breaking their software. And it wasn’t just games.
Some users found their Windows Hello PIN broke on every restart. They were
trapped in an endless loop where Windows would corrupt its own security keys. Others reported,
black screens, and broken displays. On August 20th, Microsoft officially added the game crashes
to the update’s known issues. Then came the explanation.
It was the fault of your glowing keyboard and fans.
Microsoft claimed that RGB lighting was interfering with core parts of the system.
To be fair to Microsoft, they have a valid point here. The driver these lighting utilities rely on
runs in kernel space, the most privileged level of the system. To anti-cheat software, that’s “an
exploit waiting to happen.” Lighting software with that much access is a legitimate security concern.
And when something goes wrong at that level, it goes very wrong.
If the driver is cut off in the middle of a task, the result is a critical kernel fault.
That causes Windows to show the famous blue screens of death to protect the hardware.
That’s the crash players were seeing. But look at the actual sequence of events.
Those drivers were already sitting on gaming PCs, and the games ran perfectly fine. Then Microsoft
shipped an update and the games crashed. Microsoft said it was someone else's fault.
The fix followed the same logic though. They put a block on the lighting software from loading.
Microsoft warned that turning it off could mean RGB features behaving erratically or
not working at all. Once again, a third
party’s software got switched off. If you were tempted to roll back the
update to get your laptop or PC working again, Microsoft had already laid the perfect trap.
The same patch fixes a zero-day vulnerability that attackers were already exploiting.
Users were left choosing between a PC that works and a safe PC.
The real tragedy about this was how the internet was manipulated.
When Embark’s games crashed, they blamed a Windows update. But when VLC froze, it became
part of a debate about open-source software. Same kind of problem, very different conclusion.
There was no leaked memo, no whistleblower, and no internal document showing that Microsoft set
out to break VLC. The most likely explanation is probably more boring: an overzealous security
update, a detection rule that caught a harmless file, and a company pushing monthly patches to
millions of machines, for genuinely good reasons. But that comes with an uncomfortable truth.
The absence of intent doesn't matter. Microsoft owns the operating system. It
owns the antivirus that scans your files. It owns the browser your links open in,
the media player waiting in the wings when VLC stumbles, and the store that hands its own apps
the paved road. When one company controls every layer, a strategic attack and an accidental bug
look exactly the same from your chair… Because they end in the same place.
Jonathan Blow is the proof. No plan was needed. One bad update, one frustrating wait,
and a respected developer publicly moved from independent software to Microsoft’s
own app. All while telling his followers that open source was the real problem.
And notice who ended up doing the fixing. The workaround didn’t come from Microsoft.
It came from the volunteers, who had to build their own tools to fix it. The company whose
update set it off didn’t have to lift a finger. Flip the roles. Imagine a free, volunteer-built
antivirus locked away a core file inside Microsoft’s Media Player, and every song suddenly
took half a minute to start. How long would it take for headlines to declare that open-source
security tools were reckless and embarrassing? The asymmetry is the story. When Microsoft breaks
something, it’s just a bug. When anyone else is caught in the blast radius, it’s their fault.
The people who pay the price are volunteer projects with no PR department and no hotline
to corporate headquarters. They’re the ones having to answer public accusations on their own time.
And the tools they build, like VLC, are often the very first things people install to make a
new Windows PC feel like their own. Because when a company that builds
your operating system also decides which software looks suspicious,
which links open where, and which drivers get shut off, independent software never stands a chance.
And when Microsoft breaks your computer, it’s the volunteer who has to shoulder the blame.
